title: Four Easy Tricolour Recipes to Celebrate Independence Day 2026
excerpt: From tiranga ravioli to phirnee, these chef-recommended dishes bring the saffron, white, and green of the Indian flag to your kitchen table this August 15.
body:
• Professional chefs share four tricolour recipes—ravioli, pastry, coconut ladoo, and phirnee—that use natural ingredients to recreate the Indian flag's colours
  • Each recipe can be prepared in under 90 minutes and works for both experienced cooks and beginners
  • Diaspora families can adapt these dishes with ingredients available at Indian grocery stores across the US, UK, and Canada

As India marks its 80th Independence Day on August 15, 2026, kitchens across the country and the diaspora are turning patriotic. Professional chefs have shared easy-to-follow tricolour recipes that bring the saffron, white, and green of the Tiranga to the dining table—dishes that are as much about celebration as they are about taste.

Tiranga Ravioli

Chef Sachin Malik, Executive Chef at Radisson Blu MBD Hotel in Noida, offers a fusion take with tricolour ravioli. The dish uses three separate doughs—plain semolina for white, beetroot paste for saffron-orange, and spinach paste for green—layered together with egg wash between each sheet.

The ravioli are filled with a stuffing of your choice, cut into squares with a pastry cutter, dried for an hour, then boiled in salted water for 10 to 15 minutes. Served with sauce and grated cheese, the layered pasta reveals the three colours of the flag when cut open. The recipe requires 250g semolina, 250g refined flour, 12 egg yolks, 100g each of beetroot and spinach paste, plus salt.

Tricolour Coconut Ladoo

For a simpler sweet option, Chef Swapnadeep Mukherjee recommends tricolour coconut ladoo. The recipe calls for coconut powder, condensed milk, purified butter, and regular milk. The coconut powder is roasted in butter for five minutes on low flame, then milk and condensed milk are added and stirred until thick.

The mixture is divided into three parts: one tinted orange with food-grade colour, one green, and one left white. Rolled into small balls with soft hands and layered in order, the ladoo look like miniature flags and can be served warm or cold.

Tiranga Pastry

Chef Malik also shares a tricolour pastry that works well for parties. Using eggless cake mix (1 kg), the batter is split into three parts and tinted orange, green, and white before baking separately at 180°C for 15 minutes each. A buttercream icing made from 300g unsalted butter and 300g icing sugar is similarly divided and coloured.

The cooled sponge layers are stacked and decorated with the matching icings, then cut into pastry-sized pieces. The result is a layered dessert that reveals the tricolour with every slice.

Tiranga Phirnee

The most traditional option is tiranga phirnee, a three-layered rice pudding. Basmati rice is soaked for 30 minutes, then coarsely ground. Full-fat milk is boiled and thickened on low flame before the ground rice is stirred in continuously to avoid lumps.

Once the rice is cooked, sugar, rose water, and cardamom powder are added. The pudding is divided into three portions: one topped with grated carrot and saffron for orange, one garnished with crushed almonds for white, and one finished with pistachios for green. Served chilled in earthen cups, the phirnee carries the colours of the flag in layers.

"Preparing and sharing a patriotic dish on this day reinforces unity in diversity, respect for democratic values, and gratitude for sacrifices made."

— Dr. Kaviraj Khialani, Celebrity Master Chef

Tips for Diaspora Kitchens

All four recipes use ingredients readily available at Indian grocery stores in the US, UK, and Canada. Basmati rice, condensed milk, semolina, and food-grade colours are staples at stores like Patel Brothers, India Bazaar, and online retailers. For natural colouring, beetroot and spinach work as dye-free alternatives to artificial food colours.

Independence Day celebrations in diaspora communities often centre around community gatherings and cultural events. These dishes travel well and can be prepared ahead of time—the ladoo and phirnee in particular improve with a few hours of chilling.
